conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the weight of evidence supports a "no" answer, stating that benzodiazepines and Z-drugs have not been proven to cause Alzheimer's or other forms of dementia and attributing observed associations to confounding and reverse causation. Therefore, it rejects the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
The evidence is mixed, but your answer of "no" is supported by several rigorous analyses that attribute the apparent association to confounding and reverse causation.

**Observational associations:** Some case-control and population studies have linked benzodiazepine use to higher dementia risk. A 2014 case-control study found past benzodiazepine use associated with a 43–51% increased Alzheimer's risk, rising with dose and duration (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4159609/). A 2025 case-control study reported a 65% higher dementia risk, with long half-life agents doubling risk versus short-acting ones (https://www.jns-journal.com/article/S0022-510X(25)00366-1/fulltext). Similarly, high cumulative zolpidem doses have been linked to increased Alzheimer's risk in older adults (https://agsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jgs.15018).

**Confounding and reverse causation:** However, these associations are widely questioned. Benzodiazepines are prescribed for anxiety and insomnia—symptoms that often precede dementia diagnosis, creating "protopathic bias" (medication given for early prodromal symptoms). A 2025 study found that the association disappeared after controlling for confounding, concluding benzodiazepines "do not appear to be a significant risk factor for dementia" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167494325001086). A meta-analysis of sedative-hypnotics found no association with dementia except for benzodiazepines, and even that association "did not persist after exclusion of studies with potential reverse causation and confounding by indication" (https://discovery.dundee.ac.uk/en/publications/use-of-sedative-hypnotic-medications-and-risk-of-dementia-a-syste). A 2022 USC study found little evidence that older adults prescribed benzodiazepines face increased dementia risk (https://schaeffer.usc.edu/research/benzodiazepines-dont-increase-dementia-risks-in-older-adults-usc-study-finds/). Two separate expert reviews concluded benzodiazepine use does not cause dementia (https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp.2020.20040375).

**Clinical caution:** Despite the lack of proven causation, the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria still recommends avoiding benzodiazepines in adults 65+ due to cognitive impairment, falls, and fractures (https://agsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jgs.18372).

**Conclusion:** The current weight of evidence supports your answer—benzodiazepines and Z-drugs have not been proven to cause Alzheimer's or other dementias. The observed associations likely reflect confounding by indication and reverse causation, though long-term cognitive side effects warrant caution.
